analysis.investment_thesis: Vandan Foods screens optically cheap at P/E 2.95 but the 0.53% ROE signals dismal returns on capital — the Magic Formula requires BOTH cheapness and quality, and this fails the quality test decisively. A castor oil commodity processor with sub-1% ROE is not a business Greenblatt would touch regardless of valuation.
key_strengths: Low headline P/E of 2.95 suggests high earnings yield optically
Promoter holding of 66.42% shows owner alignment
Niche in castor oil derivatives (India is global leader in castor)
key_risks: ROE of 0.53% implies near-zero return on capital — fails Magic Formula quality leg
Tiny market cap (INR 26.60 Cr) means illiquidity and likely earnings volatility
Commodity edible-oil business with no pricing power or moat
red_flags: ROE <1% is a disqualifier — P/E may reflect one-time earnings, not sustainable EBIT
Micro-cap with no disclosed EBIT/EV or capital-employed data to verify ROIC
Possible SME/recent listing (symbol 544436) with limited operating history at scale
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks stocks on earnings yield (EBIT/EV) and return on capital (EBIT/(NWC+NFA)). At P/E 2.95 with INR 26.60 Cr market cap, implied earnings are ~INR 9 Cr and earnings yield looks superficially attractive. However, ROE of 0.53% is catastrophic — the "cheapness" is likely illusory, driven by a non-recurring gain or an inflated equity base. Return on capital in castor oil processing is structurally low: working-capital heavy, commodity pricing, thin margins.

Greenblatt explicitly wants companies that earn high returns on tangible capital — that's the "good business" half of the formula. A 0.53% ROE means capital is being deployed at below risk-free rates; no multiple of cheapness compensates for that. Combined with the tiny float, commodity exposure, and lack of verifiable capital-employed data, this fails both the quantitative screen and the common-sense quality filter. Pass.
